utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Since we discussed all practical problems yesterday when we were to adjourn, I think we immediately can continue, Ms. Pilipovic, with the cross-examination of Mr. Harding. No, Mr. Ierace is on his feet. Please, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. There is an issue I would seek to raise briefly before we recommence the cross-examination of Mr. Harding. It relates to the evidence of Berko Zecevic. He is to be called following Mr. Kucanin, and [redacted]. Mr. President, in the 65 ter summary for Berko Zecevic, the Prosecution has described him as a highly-qualified expert in heavy weapons technology. And indeed the Prosecution relies on part of his evidence as that of an expert witness. That, then, automatically raises the relevant rule, which is 94 bis. Mr. President, that rule was amended in December of 2001. It requires under 94 bis (a) that the statement be disclosed within a time limit prescribed by the Trial Chamber. Firstly, in relation to that, there are two statements by this witness, the first was disclosed in the year 2000, and that is the statement upon which the Prosecution relies. There is also a report upon which the Prosecution relies, and that has also been disclosed in mid-2000. There is another statement which has been disclosed in the last few days made by this witness. The Prosecution does not rely on any of the material in that statement. It has simply been disclosed as part of our obligations under reciprocal disclosure. Moving on to 94 bis (b), the Trial Chamber is required to -- withdraw that. Within a particular period of time of the filing of the statement, that is, 30 days, or such other time prescribed by the Trial Chamber, the Defence in this case is required to file a notice indicating whether it accepts the expert witness statement or it wishes to cross-examine the expert witness. And if the statement of the expert witness, this is under 94 bis (c), if the Defence in this case accepts the expert witness's statement, then it may be admitted into evidence by the Trial Chamber without the witness being called. Mr. President, that is the decision which is required by the Rule. I indicate for the Prosecution that we do not submit that the Defence need in these circumstances to file a notice indicating whether it accepts the expert witness statement or whether it wishes to cross-examine the expert witness. I say that because the 65 ter summary for this witness did not carry a heading that he was an expert witness; rather it's apparent from the text. So in short, the Prosecution is content for this witness to be called in the ordinary way and to be cross-examined in the ordinary way. If my learned colleague prefers that this issue be raised in the presence of Mr. Piletta-Zanin, then I am content to raise it again tomorrow. But I thought it best to raise it at the first opportunity that I became aware of it as a potential issue so as to give maximum notice to the Trial Chamber and the Defence. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ierace. Ms. Pilipovic. You see, Mr. Harding, we still have some procedural issues to deal with you. I beg for your patience. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Good morning to everyone. The Defence has understood what our learned friend has just said. We understand the essence of the issue. The Defence, however, would like to acquaint itself in greater detail with Mr. Zekovic's statement. I wish to mention that we are referring to statements and not to an expert opinion. In any case, before the start of the cross-examination tomorrow, the Defence will set out its position with reference to Mr. Zekovic's testimony after consulting Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. So then for the time being, the order will not change as we see it now. I've one additional question to you, although I have not the new text of 94 bis, which has not yet in a -- you have it -- because the consolidated form is not there. It is there, but...

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I also have a spare copy if you...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll just have a look at. Yes, I see that especially the necessity which did exist under Rule 94 bis to file the statement of an expert witness is not contained any more in 94 bis (a) so that I have no question any more. Thank you, Mr. Ierace. So then, Ms. Pilipovic, I think you could continue the cross-examination, or to -- for you, it's start your part of the cross-examination of the witness, Mr. Harding. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Harding, good morning. Can you tell us whether on the 31st of May, 2001, you talked to the investigators of the prosecution and made a statement regarding the events that took place during your stay in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that's the date of the statement, then yes. I do not have a copy of the statement in front of me, but I was questioned by an investigator, Jonathan Tait-Harris.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Mr. Harding, you are an infantry officer. Did you tell us what military schools you went to and when you graduated from those schools?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I reported to the Royal Air Force college at Cromwell on the 30th of October, 1982. I graduated from that college on the 14th of March, 1983, and I graduated as a second lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: From there, I commenced flying training as a pilot --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, I think we usually have both the microphones on. Yes.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the Royal Air Force College, I then started pilot training within the Royal Air Force. And after a year of that pilot training, I then failed the course. Then I had to resign my contract, and then in 1985, I rent to Royal Air Force to be trained as an RAF officer. When I finished that course at the end of that year, I had to do another course on armoured vehicles. When I finished that, I then reported to my first operational unit at RAF Akcroteri in Cyprus. I did two years at Cyprus. I then did another operational tour --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You have explained to us what schools you went to. Can you tell us how it happened that you, as an infantry officer, were transferred to the RAF?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within the Royal Air Force is the RAF regiment. It is part of the air force. We use army tactics and equipment, and we are part of the air force, commanded by the air force, and so I've always been in the air force.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us while you were studying to be an infantry officer, what kind of weapons you studied in detail and what kind of weapons you gained only superficial information about?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the initial mission [phoen] Course at RAF Catrick is all small arms operated by the airforce just from small pistol which the pilots would have up to a 7.62 millimetre sustained fire machine-gun, which is on a tripod. Before I went to Sarajevo, 12 months previous, I had undergone another course which was the use of artillery, target information, adjustments of targets for mortars and artillery, and also tank target indication. That was then reinforced with a course on forward air controlling to bring aircraft weapon systems on to targets. So I had used --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. And during your training, which you said lasted a year, what weapons did you personally aim out of and which did you only watch being used?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had the siting target indication in use because I was an officer of captain rank of 105 millimetre artillery, which is called the light gun. And the 155 millimetre artillery, and also the 81 millimetre mortar. Added to that was an anti-tank weapons. So we were siting, controlling, ordering the fire of and adjusting the fire of all of those weapon systems as commissioned officers, platoon commanders, and company commanders.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Harding, you have told us that a year before your arrival in Sarajevo, you underwent training. You told us that you were trained in the use of weapons. Can you tell us whether you were also trained specifically for your mission in Sarajevo and what sort of training this was.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: The specific training before I arrived was I reported to Zagreb. We had the Canadian engineers. They ran through all of the mines that were in use. And at that time, the mines they used were all live because there was no training equipment. We went through vehicles, radios, reports, all the administration required by UNPROFOR at that time. And that's the training that I had in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, you told us you arrived in Sarajevo in late July and that you were assigned as an UNMO to PAPA 1 on the mill -- hill of Hum. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what task you were given when you were assigned to PAPA 1?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: My task there was to observe and report all military activity that could be seen from the position. I was also there to monitor the activity of the 105 millimetre Howitzers that were dug in at that location.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday, in response to a question by my learned friend at 9.33, you said that your job as an UNMO was to observe all military activities on both sides. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: The task of the UNMOs was to monitor both sides. From my position, I could only monitor the one side, but the LIMA call signs monitored the other side, and the information was collated by the PTT staff in the PTT building on telecoms.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You are telling us, therefore, that in the performance of your duties, and we are now referring to PAPA 1, it was your duty to observe only the positions of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that it was your duty to report what was happening on that line. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was my duty to report all military activity that I could see from that position. So I could see across the valley on to the other side, and if I saw activity on the other side, then also I would also report that. It is not necessarily just the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina; it's also the Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you arrived at PAPA 1, where were you accommodated and were your lodgings in the same place as your observation post?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we lived in a house on the ground floor about 50 to 75 metres from the first weapon.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And in that building, what were you able to see from there? Were you able to see the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina positions from there?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the house, we could see across the valley, but the observation position was around by the guns which gave a much better view across the city, although sitting on a target, we had to be careful. But it was a much better observation post. All four guns were dug in and were behind an earth bank so they couldn't be seen from the other side. So I would observe from the house and also from the gun positions.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Harding, when you arrived at PAPA 1, were you told what your role as an UNMO was, and by this I mean what did you actually observe? What military formation were you given the task of observing?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was observing the artillery battery and its 50 troops, but I was reporting all military activity. One of my first reports was a small-arms fire fight in Tito barracks, which was in the city, and also I reported an air attack off to the west at some distance. That's to give an example of the types of activity that I would report. It was not who was doing what; it was more what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Harding, I will come back to your methods of work and reporting later. Now, I would like to return to the observation on the hill of Hum. Were you aware of the positions of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina on that hill, and did you know what military formation was on the hill of Hum? When you were given your task, were you also provided with this information regardless of what you found when you got there?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only information I was given was a location of that artillery. I wasn't briefed on any other position anywhere on the hill. It was solely that one position.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether your positions --- and by that, I'm referring to PAPA 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6 --- whether they were located in certain areas of the town where there were brigades? Was this the practice in setting up observation posts in the territories held by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was involved in the relocation of all of the PAPA sites to make them observation posts. The siting was done with regard to the ground that we could see. Once we knew where we wanted to put the observation post, we would then need to find out in what area it was and what brigade, and therefore go through the 1st Corps, and then get permission to put it up there, and then do the administration after that. Whilst we sited it, it was not with regard to any brigade boundaries, but it was with regard to the front line at the time and possible withdrawal of our troops should it be needed. But no brigade lines were ever considered because we didn't draw tactical maps of either side because we were not there to assess their tactics. It was merely to observe the city.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether on your arrival at your post as an UNMO you were acquainted with the topography of the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I arrived, we had one or two days in the UN headquarters, which was in the PTT building, and we were just briefed from maps so you could see the valley. And then once we were given the maps, it was up to us to acquaint ourselves with the layout of the city.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what hills and mountains surround the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: To do that, accurately, I would do it from a map. Because we didn't number the hills or anything. It was just by the names on the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission, the Defence would like to show the witness a map that he has already had the opportunity to see. And I should like to ask him to mark for us the mountains around Sarajevo and also the elevations around the town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's the map that was used yesterday during examination-in-chief. Mr. Harding, all marking done at the request of the Defence will be done in black marker pen. So I saw the blue one already in your hand. Mr. Usher, could you please give the map to the witness and perhaps assist him in keeping the map flat on the ELMO surface.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, would you please indicate for us the Hum hill on this map. I believe that you have already marked it. I think you've marked it with number 1.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: The actual peak of the hill is directly north from the triangle and the number 1. We were down from the peak of it. We were not right on top. Would you like me to mark the peak, or are you happy that it's directly north?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: That's quite sufficient, thank you. Could you then indicate for us other hills on this map. Perhaps the Grdonja hill.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: To do it by name is very difficult for me because it's nearly ten years ago. We did all of our work from the map at the time. When we referred to a hill, we used a 6-figure grid reference. If near to that location there was a name on the map, we would also state that because that assists the person who is plotting the 6-figure grid reference. We always referred to 6-figure grid references because some of us could not pronounce correctly the locations on the map, and it was common military practice to use grid references.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Harding, can you tell us in what part of the town the Grdonja hill is situated?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say again that we referred to grid references, not to mountain ranges by name. I can draw the ridges that I could observe from PAPA 1. But it was all done by grid reference.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission, I should like to ask the witness to mark for us the elevations around Sarajevo. Since this seems to be a problem on this map, could we perhaps use another map and then have the witness mark this map? I could perhaps assist the witness. We have a copy of a Prosecution exhibit indicating the PAPA positions in Sarajevo. Maybe that would assist the witness so that he can indicate for us all of the elevations surrounding the town of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for my information, Ms. Pilipovic, are you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. testing whether the witness is aware of the location of the ridges, or is it for any other reasons that you'd like to find out where these ridges are? I'm not quite certain about which part of Rule 98 we are at this very moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, during the examination-in-chief, the witness spoke about the positions and locations from where the BH army soldiers opened fire. And also, the positions that were sources of the activity and fire of the Serb army. In the statements given to the OTP, the witness did not mention the fact that all major elevations were held by the army of Republika Srpska, and that there was a small number of elevations held by the BH army. With my questions, first of all, I wish to test the credibility of the witness and furthermore I think that for the purposes of assessing the value of this testimony it is important to establish what the elevations were held by the BH army and what were the elevations held by the VRS so that I can follow up with appropriate questions. I think that we should first establish that. If the witness does not know the Zuc hill or the Grdonja hill or Mount Igman, Trebevic or Mojmilo, let him say so. But if he can mark these locations on a map, I think that that would be of considerable assistance to all of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do better understand what your questions will be about. Would that mean that you'll ask him to identify certain hills or would you like to have him identify all the hills around which seem to be part of the question? What map are you going to use?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it will be very useful for the Defence for the witness to identify all of the hills in view of what he was doing in Sarajevo. And also, to tell us with respect of his testimony in chief from what positions the artillery and rocket launchers were active. I'm referring to the VRS positions. For me to be able to follow up with these questions, I need the witness to mark for us these specific locations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic. And what map do you intend to use for that purpose?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I've made a copy of the PAPA position. This is a Prosecution exhibit, and I think that it might assist the witness to tell us specifically what elevations and hills around Sarajevo were relevant in this respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it is a document, I assume, which is not known yet to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, again, this is a Prosecution exhibit, and I've made a sufficient number of copies. It is the document 0062165. I've made copies for my colleagues as well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be given the number D53.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you recognise this map?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the first time I've seen it. But to answer your questions, would you like me to draw the front lines on this map, rather than name the hills? I can show you Zuc, I can show Igman. These were large areas and there were military operations in that general area. But I can draw the front line all the way around the city, and from that you can decide who has the high ground and who doesn't. But you would need to specify what front line you would want because when I arrived in August 1992, there was one front line. But the time I left, there were some significant changes as Bosnian Serb army had gained ground and in other areas, the forces within the city had also gained ground. It changed. So if you specify the time, either January 1993 or August 1992. Which one would you like?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Harding, we would like you to mark for us, if possible, the front line as it was at the time of your arrival at PAPA 1. So August 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you also assist the witness in such a way that we can see on our screen exactly what he is marking. So if you'd please try to keep the -- his hands on our screens.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, could you tell us what you're marking at this particular moment so that we can understand.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: With a black pen with a constant line I'm marking the approximate location of the front line. In some areas, it was quite a ground to be classed as no-man's-land as it gave cover to neither side. So it's not going to be exact because it was effectively natural buffer zones caused by the lie of the land. But this is the approximate location that if we were to go near it, we would have to liaise with one or both sides because we would be going into an area of a possible conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that's July 1992 upon your arrival?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I go around, do you want me to highlight the major hills of consideration?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, what you have just marked for us on PA and PB, is the front line held by whom, which army?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the north and to the west is the Bosnian Serb army. Inside is the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I only dealt with forces on the inside. In my entire time I had nothing to do with the Serbian side as that was within the LIMA call signs.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Just one more question concerning this particular area. Do you have any knowledge as to the presence of the 2nd Motorised Brigade in this area, the area that you marked with PA and PB, the BH army? Was this area covered by the 2nd Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: The area of PAPA 5A and PAPA 5B, we were there as observers. We did liaise with the military personnel or the local commanders. But as I said, it was not our task to draw tactical maps, and therefore we only referred to our call signs and not any military formation, be it mechanised brigade or just infantry brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge about the strength of this brigade? What was the number of troops?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, that is tactical information, and it was not our role to find out numbers. We would report equipment, but we would not report or record that sort of tactical information. The reason we didn't do that was that if I needed to go on to the other side, be it either way, LIMA come to me or I go outside, if I was closely questioned, I would not know that information. And that was the agreements that we had in order for us to move around the city.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You've just told us that you had contact with military personnel and local commanders. Could you be perhaps a bit more precise? What military personnel and what military commanders were you in contact with in this area, PAPA PA and PB

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: PAPA 5 Alpha and Bravo, it would be the commander of the forces there. We would be told who was in command. We would then go to find him. We would then ask him where the dangerous spots where such as snipers and basically where we would -- we should not go to endanger ourselves. By military personnel, it was purely the commander at the time. He may or may not have had military training.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us where it was that you spoke to local commanders and can you name one of them? Also, can you name anyone from the military personnel and tell us where they were quartered in this area?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. We did liaise with the military commander whose headquarters was by PAPA 5 Alpha. It was near the end of this salient. I cannot give you his name as we just referred to them as local commanders, but he was right next to the accommodation area, which is at A. The observation post is at B. But that is where he was barracked and did his operations from.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Are you telling us that the headquarters of the military personnel you had contact with and those of the local commanders were situated near the observation post PAPA A?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: PAPA 5A was the accommodation. It was not an observation post. But his building was just down the street.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you describe for us the type of buildings that the local commanders were accommodated in, those that you had contact with, as well as the military personnel?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: The buildings in this area were made of concrete and breeze block. 80 per cent of them had been finished. There was hardly any population left here because it was subject to fire from the north, from the west, and also from the east. It was considered to be the most dangerous position for us. But they were in the finished and also unfinished buildings in this area. 5A is in an unfinished building which is a concrete frame, whereas 5B is in a concrete frame only. 5A was in a completely finished house.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Is it your testimony that you were accommodated in residential blocks, and that that was the case of the local commanders and military personnel of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. During what period of time did you stay and how often at PAPA A position?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stayed at PAPA 5 only once, because shortly after that it was withdrawn because it was considered too dangerous, and also it did not interlink with the other observation posts that we wanted in the city. It couldn't see what we needed it to see, and it was too dangerous. So I stayed there at the beginning of August 1992. The accommodation was during the day and the observation post was manned at night.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, when PAPA A and B were withdrawn? At what period of time, in which month?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Without reference to the diary, I would suspect that they were moved in September, late September. Maybe. I cannot be certain of that because all of the positions were being moved around, and there were administration considerations. So an observation post, although chosen, could not be operated immediately because we had to sort out who owned the house and also liaise with people around and also make sure that it could achieve what we wanted it to achieve.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Thank you. You told us a moment ago that you could mark for us the hills dominating the town of Sarajevo on this map, the hills that you know about. Could you indicate that for us now, please.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm marking the front line that was known to me in August 1992. To the north of it is the area of Zuc. There was some significant activity in this area. And later on in my time in Sarajevo, and I just marked the general area of Zuc on top of where it is written on the map. The black continuous line has joined the dotted blue line because the dotted blue line was the front line that we discussed yesterday as part of the Prosecution. So I won't overwrite it so it still remains clear if that's okay. Is that okay?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, now that you have indicated this part of the map and put the dotted blue line there, in response to a question of my learned friend, you mentioned the 9th Motorised Brigade of the BH army, and you told us that it also encompassed the area of seven woods that can be seen on the map. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't refer to any formed unit as in mechanised brigades. There would be concentrations of troops because we did not record tactical information such as that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you mark for us the concentration of troops in this area? You told my learned colleague where the front line of the BH army was, so in respect -- with respect to that area, could you tell us where the BH army positions in the area of Grdonja hill were and the area of seven woods, that is where the troops were concentrated?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. There are four questions in one, if they could be broken down into separate pieces just to assist the Trial Chamber. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, could you please split it up.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you have marked a line as a response to a question put to you by my learned colleague. Now, as the extension of that line is, can you mark the area of the Grdonja hill with respect to that line and tell us whether you have any knowledge about the presence of the BH army troops in the area of Grdonja hill.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later on in my time in Sarajevo, we positioned PAPA 6 which was marked yesterday and the pen is pointing to it south of the city on a steep slope.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: From that observation post, we can observe to the north, and then could see this hill and the front lines on it. So from my position at PAPA 1, at the time that we're talking about, August 1992, I would not have any knowledge of the military operations up here. That is why we put in PAPA 6, because although we could hear things were going on, we could see casualties arriving at the hospital but we had no idea what was going on. That's why PAPA 6 was put in as discussed yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There has been a misunderstanding and confusion. The Witness was referring to the observation post number 6.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: The way I understand you said that it was from observation post number 6 that you were able to observe the Grdonja hill and six woods. You tried to explain to us where the observation post 6 was and what could be seen from that post, what troops could be seen from that post.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. But there is a problem with the time line. We're talking August 1992 when I was at PAPA 1 or PAPA 5 when we didn't know what was going on here or in October, November 1992 when PAPA 6 was put in here, and then we started to report. August 1992, I cannot state what troop concentrations there were especially by unit and also by words which are not particularly clear on this map. This front line that I'm drawing is, to the best of my knowledge, was accurate for August 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you mark that part of the front line on the map now, I mean August 1992.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, could you please tell us whether you have marked the front line where the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina troops were concentrated, that is, their positions?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've marked the front line which would be basically no-man's-land. For example, I'm pointing to an area just to the west of the PTT building and slightly east of the area Otes which was discussed yesterday. This is flat river plain, so it belonged to neither side. It could be covered by fire from one side or the other. The troops would be dug in in buildings, and where this protection would not be out on the plain, so this line does not designate the forward edge of troops from either side. It was merely the no-man's-land. It includes the area of Otes, goes through Ilidza. I've drawn a question mark here as I'm not certain of where the front line went just to the north of the airfield. It's the no-man's-land I've marked, not formation of troops, trenches, gun positions and other such like.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether in the part that you marked Otes, whether the HVO and the 102nd Motorised Brigade of the army of BH was?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: The area of Otes to us was a group of buildings that we observed on the observation post PAPA 5. I personally never went into that area as it was observed from PAPA 5. So I could not tell you what equipment was in there and other such things because we didn't go into Otes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you mark on the map in relation to Igman where this was? Whether Igman is left of Ilidza and Otes.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the map at the moment you can see the main airport with its primary runway running up there. If I draw the front line south and west of the airport, the area south and to the west of the airport, this area is known as Mount Igman. I've written it on the map in black pen. The steeply rising ground and was all covered in woods. The town of Butmir belonged to or was under the control of the Bosnian-Herzegovina army. The Serb army had control of the open ground to the west of Otes and on the flat lands. Again, I cannot guarantee this front line. This is purely from the knowledge knowing that Butmir was not under Serb control. Ilidza was always a source of conflict, and Otes, in August 1992, did not belong to the Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that Ilidza was always a source of conflict, can you tell us whose forces were there and what concentration of forces was present on Igman?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first part of your question, Ilidza was a built-up area and had forces from both sides. I say by a lot of activity in that from PAPA 5 we were constantly reporting incoming fire landing on Ilidza. The actual numbers of the troops there from either side, I could not say because we did not go down into Ilidza. LIMA call signs may have more information on that area. The second part of the question is Mount Igman. I personally only went there once, and it was for a meeting with the brigade commanders on Mount Igman with a view to putting a PAPA observation post on Mount Igman. Although we had discussions, in the end we did not achieve any agreements, and I only went there once.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us with what commander did you negotiate on Mount Igman with respect to opening a PAPA point there?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our first point of contact was with Brigade Commander. It was of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. a cause of concern for us, and I also think the Bosnian Army, his name something like Juka. We were with him for only 10 minutes, and then we were taken to a building that had been used for the Winter Olympics. There we met some of the other brigade commanders, but I couldn't give you their names as I did not record it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, were you able to see the weapons that were there on Igman, the weapons of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina? Did you see guns, Howitzers?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only weapons I saw were the small arms carried by the troops. For example, Juka and the eight men that were with him were extremely well-equipped; however, they did seem to have marginal military training. To get to him, I saw one T-34 tank which had been taken out of action. When we were taken to the buildings, we were not given any guided tour or any information on the types of weapons that were up there. We did try to find out because there had been reports of heavy weapons firing from Mount Igman into areas occupied by the Serb army, but we were unsuccessful at finding out exactly where they were. We were there to try and agree on an observation post. If we happened to see the weapons, we would have recorded it. But we didn't because of it is very dense forest, and we didn't really go anywhere in the vehicle we had. We were in an UN armoured vehicle so its passage was restricted anyway by its size.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Harding, while conducting your mission as an UNMO, did you draw up reports on your daily activities in the field, you and the others working with you, and were these reports made up daily or weekly?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did record what happened. The first instance, there were three forms we could use. The first one would be an incident report, which was abbreviated to INTREP, and that would be where military activity had been seen, but could not be attributed to either side. We then had a form called a sit -- ShootRep which was to report outgoing fire near to one of our positions or from a position that could be identified. The final form was called a BombRep which was in we were shelled or if we could identify a specific area that was being shelled. These forms were filled out at the time of observation. They were reported to PAPA headquarters. PAPA headquarters would then collate that information and forward it to the UN headquarters housed within the PTT building. That collation was done once a week. Then the senior military office would collate the information and other activities for the entire month, would write out a report and would send it to the main UN headquarters for the area which eventually became in Kiseljak, although he collated the LIMA and PAPA side as we had no contact with each other.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the course of your work as an UNMO, did you receive protests by either side, either the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina or the army of Republika Srpska, or the members of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps on activity in certain parts of town or in areas falling within PAPA 1 or 3 or 5, so did you get any protests?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, protests were received. Their route was through the liaison officers in the PTT building. I personally did not receive complaints because that was not the route they needed to go. If our positions were shelled, we would then put a complaint on to the side that we estimated had fired the shells. So yes, complaints in the PTT, not to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you are telling us that if positions were shelled, positions of the army of Republika Srpska, if Ilidza or Lukavica were shelled from Igman, the complaints would be received by LIMA observers, not by you?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we observed the shelling which we did in those areas, we would then report it using the forms I've specified. If there were to be a complaint, it may well have gone through LIMA call signs or it was through the Serbian army liaison team that was directly in the PTT building. I personally know that when there was a complaint it didn't come through me; it went straight to my higher command. I can't answer for the LIMA side.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I think you said that Mr. Richard Mole was your superior officer at some point and then later on Mr. Cutler. Are they the persons who received reports from PAPA and from LIMA?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Lieutenant Colonel Richard Mole and Lieutenant Colonel Cutler with my direct senior officers and they collated information from both sides. So he would be my point of contact to find out about a complaint. The route above him and within the PTT was not known to me. But it would be conveyed to me through the colonel.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you were marking these positions and the front line on the map, you told us that was in August 1992. Can you tell us whether these lines shifted and whether in the period while you were on duty, that is, from August to the 23rd of January, 1993, did these lines shift and was there fighting in certain parts of town? Do you know that in December 1992, there was fighting on the hill of Zuc?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: To answer the first part of your question, yes, the front lines did change significantly and that is why I asked the time line for the front line that I drew on the map. There was a lot of fighting in Zuc, and the Bosnian army pushed out of Sarajevo and gained ground. Conversely, there was a large battle around Otes where the Serbian army gained ground and the front line moved. Other areas of the front line were very static because the ground was very difficult, which is basically on the south side of town where it is very, very steep and closely wooded and the road that went to Pale was a significant boundary for both sides.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You have just told us that the hill of Hum, the hill of Zuc, and Mount Igman were under the control of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And in the case of Zuc, there was fighting, and it was under the army of BH control from December 1992. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the front line moved out to the northwest of the city, and fighting -- although I'm unsure who initiated the fighting. But by the ground that was gained, I would presume it's from the army that I was observing on my side of the line.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Harding, can you tell us the following: You talked about fighting for Otes, fighting for Zuc. Can you tell us how long, for how many days the fighting for Zuc went on? This was in December, but can you tell us for how many days they fought?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally did not record it in my diary, but from my best recollection, it was for at least three to four days as it was covered on the television and the reporting was from -- mainly from the LIMA side because to the north it was over the ridge line and could not be observed from PAPA 5 or PAPA 2 as we were all looking inside. We also did not have any liaison teams moving out as the front line moved, although later on in my time I did go on to some of the ground that was gained from the push out to the northwest, but I did not go far enough to locate the new front line.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether in this fighting, and I'm referring to the fighting on Zuc and Otes in December, the fighting you've just been referring to, do you know whether the two armies taking part were the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the army of -- the Serbian army, and it was the forces within Sarajevo that initiated the fighting out. I hesitate to call them an army because I did watch troop movements going northeast, some had uniforms, some did not, but they all wore the same coloured armband on their left arm.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the armband worn on the left arm of members of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, what it designated?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: We presumed that it would designate that they were the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Some of them had the uniform pattern from the former JNA, and we presumed it was to avoid confusion if they were to advance north on to the front line and meet Serb army forces that I presumed would wear that sort of uniform. I did not have any close contact with the Serbian army personnel so I couldn't say for sure, but they all wore it. It was not a rank designation, and as far as we could see, it was not a unit designation.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware whether in the fighting for Otes and Zuc there were any casualties and what the number of casualties was?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were casualties on both sides. The fighting at Zuc was covered by a television team, nationality I do not know, but we did see on the television that they were showing casualties and they were very vivid scenes. The battle for Otes, there were casualties. Some of these casualties were seen at the citizen and Kosevo Hospital as once they had been sorted out by medical personnel, they wanted to get back to Otes. I also spoke to the commander that was in Otes at the time, and he explained to me the number of weapons, type of weapons, and what the situation was like. It was witnessed by personnel from Allied Press and they would be able to tell you exactly how many casualties there were. That is a civilian press team.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Harding, can you tell us the following: During the fighting and the military operations in the fighting for Otes, to what extent was the front line involved and to what extent was it possible for fire to extend to other parts of the town not directly involved in the fighting?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: When viewed from PAPA 5, the area of Otes could clearly be seen designated by buildings. All the attacks were on to that area of buildings as it was countryside all the way around it. If I could look to the map, if you could look to the map, you'll see from yesterday there was a square drawn in blue ink with "OT" written on it. You can see to the north it is open ground and moving around to the east there's open ground although there are a few buildings. To the southwest is open ground. The only area that is -- that has got a lot of buildings is separated by this railway line. And so Otes could clearly be seen as a single area, be it suburb or village, as it was surrounded on three sides by open ground and then the railway. So it was clear to see even without reference to a map what village or suburb was in conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, would this be a convenient moment to have a break?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll adjourn until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, since you're on your feet --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- tell us something.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I simply, at this stage, wanted to give notice that when Mr. Piletta-Zanin returns, I propose to raise an issue in relation to Rule 90(H)(ii). I note that there has been some discussion of the meaning of Rule 90(H)(ii) on the case of Brdjanin Talic on the 21st of February. I noticed during the break it was raised, that is, the interpretation of that Rule, by the Prosecution in the Milosevic case, and that the Trial Chamber in that case proposes to give an amplification of the requirements which are placed on the Defence when cross-examining a witness in the near future. I had intended to raise this issue before I became aware of what has occurred in either of those two other cases. So I simply put the Defence on notice and indicate to you, Mr. President, that I do propose to raise the issue in the next day or so. In particular, the obligations which are placed on the Defence to put in one form or another to each witness the elements of the witness's evidence which are contradicted by the Defence case. Perhaps that is enough said at this stage, Mr. President. But I would be grateful if upon Mr. Piletta-Zanin's return some time could be found for me to develop my submissions. There is a reason to it, which is that, in essence, if that is not done and if in the Defence case there emerges material which does, in fact, contradict the evidence in the Prosecution case, and that material was known to the Defence at the time that the witnesses gave evidence, then it is not only contrary to the rules, directly contrary in my submission, but has significant implications for the management of the trial. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace. Part of the message is that we have to do our homework, isn't it? We'll do that. Ms. Pilipovic, is there a reason to respond at this very moment? Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, no, for the moment, Your Honour. I will respond during the appropriate discussion, that is, the discussion about the Rule 90 (b).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, may I just draw your attention to the following: I'd rather do it now than after the cross-examination has been recommenced and before the next break. The Prosecution took approximately four and one quarter of an hour yesterday to examine the witness in chief, which was more than the three hours indicated before. So although it's not necessary to use all your time, but I do understand this is a very important witness for you as well. I'll allow you to use the same time. On the other hand, I would like you to keep in mind that Mr. Piletta-Zanin will need some time tomorrow as well, and therefore I don't know what your -- how you divided your questioning and how you divided the time, but I'd like you to keep in mind that the time used together by you and Mr. Piletta-Zanin should stay within the already-extended limits used by the Prosecution. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, we addressed the issue of fighting for Otes, and you spoke about it during the examination-in-chief. In December 1992, when specifically in December 1992 this fighting took place?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: The offensive started on the 2nd of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how long it lasted, how many days?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: We concluded that the battle was over to a greater extent on the 8th of December, 1992, although the main offensive was on the 2nd through to the 4th of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: As regards to the area of Otes where this fighting took place, according to your knowledge, and in your capacity of an UNMO, do you know whether the fighting affected the areas which were not involved in the offensive? That is to say, were there any consequences of this fighting for the area beyond Otes?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: From my observations at the time, the concentration of fire was restricted to Otes itself, and such was that concentration that we could see what the objectives were because Otes is clearly defined by the open ground. The area around it, I can only presume that it would have been affected by advancing troops from either side, plus logistics required to maintain those troops during combat.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: During your tour of duty in Sarajevo, in the month of October, in the area of Stupska Petlja, Nedzarici and Kasindolska Street, do you have any knowledge as to any fighting taking place? Was that fighting observed by the observers on PAPA 5?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Without reference to the records that they made, but from my own experience, I saw fighting in -- or rather impacts in the Nedzarici area, the Stup area, Stupsko Brdo and around to Dobrinja. It was very common to see impacts from artillery or heavy weapons, rather than the actual troop movements because the observation post was too far away to see individuals because they would be covered from view. But there was often conflict all the way along that line.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you, perhaps, tell us what were the reasons for the fact that in the area of Pasino Polje and Dobrinja there were no observation points?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no PAPA call signs down at that end that could see that. There was only PAPA 5 that could see the buildings as they went around to the north of the airfield, and then beyond that, I don't know what was happening behind there. That was into the area covered by LIMA.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, you told us about your arrival at the Hum hill. And you mentioned four artillery pieces of 105 calibre and the number of 50 troops. In your opinion, what kind of formation was that? What kind of military formation or unit are we talking about in this case?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: They referred to themselves as the 105 Battery. I presume that this number was taken from the calibre, rather than the order of battle of the army or the forces that they were part of. And so they were just a battery of four weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: According to your knowledge, could that have been a Howitzer battery?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, those weapons can be referred to as Howitzer, pack Howitzer, or light gun depending on your nationality.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what is the range of this weapon?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: The range would depend on the charge placed in the cartridges. The British weapons, I think they have a selection of six bags of propellant, and they would adjust the amount of propellant according to the range. If the troops had the skill to do that, then the range of those weapons which looked to be in fairly good order, although there was minor damage from small arms, I would say that they probably had a range of about 8 -- 10 to 12 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In your view, since you were present at that observation point in the area where this weapon was located, from that position, in view of the range of the weapon, was it possible to target any part of the town of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they would have been able to engage areas of the town. The eastern area was in view. The central area was in view. But they had restricted view to the west. So if they wanted to do that, if they had Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the ammunition, then yes, they could have.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: How long did you stay at this particular observation point -- post in August, ten days, the entire month, or more?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a rotation of UNMOs through the position. I personally stayed there for five days, but there was always a military observer there. When I arrived, there was two, myself and a Russian. He then moved. I was on my own for a few days before I was joined by a Norwegian, and so the pose went on. We moved around the positions, and it was from PAPA 1, I went around to PAPA 5.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any personal knowledge or any knowledge gained from your colleagues that this battery asked for munition supplies during this particular period of time? Do you know of any such requests?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they didn't ask me or any of the UNMOs, but I know that if they could have received ammunition, then they would have used it. I think there was a general request. Ammunition would have had to have been captured on the front line, so it would be reasonable to presume they had asked for it, but it wasn't through UNMOs or any part of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge as to any other potential routes or ways that were used for this purpose, for ammunition supplies? Were you personally informed about trafficking in weapons in this part of the town?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I -- later on, we gained knowledge that ammunition had been captured during a military operation and then directed to people that could use it. But as regards trafficking of ammunition or weapons, then no, they had a few small arms and that was all they had when I left.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Harding, you described for us the soldiers, that is, people who were members of a battery. You mentioned that their number was approximately 50, and you told us that they had a certain amount of weapons, 105 millimetre weapons. You also told us that some wore uniforms and some didn't. In your opinion, would they constitute a group of soldiers or a group of civilians in that position?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was unaware of any training they had had before I arrived or whilst I arrived. Looking at it in a military context, it could be described as a militia in that they had military weapons and equipment, but they had no formal training. So they were militia in that, if you're looking for a description.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Is it your testimony that this was a paramilitary formation, if I understood correctly the interpretation?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, a paramilitary organisation would be working to their own guidelines and their own objectives. A militia are personnel taken from the local population, given just enough training to use the weapons they are provided with, and then all other training could be classed as on-the-job training and experience that they would get. So they are not a paramilitary because this battery was obviously working in liaison with a headquarters somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say they were working in liaison with a headquarters somewhere, are you referring to the main headquarters of the BH army that we spoke about and where you had your headquarters as your main base?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: By headquarters, I would mean the next level up in their command structure. I did not write down the structure of the command that we are talking about because I was not there to gain tactical information. They must have been working with other units or a headquarters. It might just be a battery headquarters. Because every day, they were delivered hot food by a vehicle and were also delivered to mortar. So somewhere was supplying this battery, and it was an ordered supply at the same time every day.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Where was the headquarters of this battery located?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did not come under my remit to find out where their headquarters was. You know, I was only there to observe military activity as previously described.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but can you perhaps tell us what military formation was observed by PAPA 2, which was also in the vicinity?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: At PAPA 2, there were self-propelled artillery known as the 2S1, and there was a counterbattery radar mounted on an armoured vehicle which I do not know the designation of it. Throughout my time, to the best of my knowledge, these vehicles never moved, and there was no maintenance carried out on them, and they were further down the hill from PAPA 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many people covered this particular area? What military formation was deployed there?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were the troops as described at PAPA 1. Down at PAPA 2, there was no more than 15 people there with the vehicles. And they are the only two formations that we had any dealings with and that we saw. As we went up the road to PAPA 1, although the road continued to the summit of Hum, we did not go up there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I have a couple of more questions regarding PAPA posts, specifically PAPA 6. Did you have any problems when setting up PAPA 6 positions? I mean, you personally and your superior officer.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did. The initial problem was trying to find a location where we could put the observation post. During our initial reconnaissance, we were fired at by 12.7 millimetre machine-gun, and we had to withdraw down the hill. And we were too close to the actual front line. We then moved to the west and found the location which eventually became PAPA 6. And then all of the grid references for PAPA observation posts, I was informed that they were given to the LIMA side to give to the Serbian army so that they know exactly where we were. Within 24 hours, every OP had been engaged and fired at by either mortars or artillery, and a round of mortar landed directly on top of the building that we were using as the observation post. Fortunately, it exploded -- it was a quick fuse. As soon as it struck the building, it exploded. It didn't penetrate, and we needed sandbags to stay there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In the area where you set up the observation post number 6, were there any paramilitaries and local commanders of the Bosnian army that prevented you or made obstacles with respect to the setting up of this observation post?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before we went to the area, we spoke to our liaison in the corps headquarters to let them know what they were doing. When we got to the area, we were given a guide so as not to go too far up the hill and too close to the front line. Apart from that, there was no obstruction in setting up the observation post; however, at one time, there was a formation of militia, and they were going to do an attack up the hill behind us. That meant we were too close to a very specific operation. We withdrew the OP. The forces advanced up the hill. They took control of part of the road to Pale. They stayed there for a short while before tanks from the Serbian army advanced down the road, and they withdrew back down the hill and there was no change in the front line. Once that had finished, we then moved back. So yes, we were -- had a problem in being too close.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Is it your testimony that those forces were forces of the BH army, the troops moving towards the road?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In this area, the area below your observation post, you told us yesterday that that was the position from which one has an unobstructed view of one portion of the town of Sarajevo. Would that be the area of Colina Kapa, Velika, and Mala?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I say, we didn't go by names unless they were prominent. I do remember the first name. But we observed the area known as Stari Grad, all of the eastern parts of the city. In our left of arc was PAPA 2, so we could see him, and right of ark was the eastern end of the city. Just move the map for one moment. You can see from the map the blue circle with number 6 is the approximate location of the observation post. We can see all of Stari Grad. We can see up the hills to the crest line which was up here, and to a certain extent you could see the beginning of the valley that then goes off to the eastern end of the city. There's an old fort somewhere down here, and there's another fort higher on the hill. We could see both of those. If This area encompasses the areas that you described, then the answer would be yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Harding, in the area of Colina Kapa, Velika, and Mala and the part where your observation post was, was there a concentration of BH army troops?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you drive up to get to PAPA 6, it was very common to see personnel with weapons and an assortment of military uniform. So there were troops enroute and in the buildings north and northeast of PAPA 6. But as to their numbers and formation designations, I couldn't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said they were in buildings. Can you tell us whether the headquarters of these units were there perhaps and whether the quarters of those troops were there? Do you know what buildings these are?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually on front line, there was a trench system. It was during our initial reconnaissance we had gone that far, hence we were engaged by the heavy machine-gun. These trenches were supported by buildings made from logs that they had cut down. And the duty shift of those on duty would man the trenches and stay in the log buildings. Those off duty would be in the buildings behind. The only reason I can say that is because I have seen troops walking towards the front line, and then later on you would see different troops walking back. So there was a roster in operation, and yes, they lived in the buildings directly behind their front line.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Harding, you have told us that your PAPA locations were in the part of the city under the control of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Can you tell us with reference to this map where the elevations were that were controlled by the army of the Bosnian Serbs -- or rather, the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see at PAPA 6, this is on a steep slope facing north. If you go south, you're going uphill into the wooded area. This is high ground. You can see by the cable car from low ground to higher ground, and you've reached the road. So the area -- the high ground along this road was held by the Serbian army. And lower down the slopes was controlled by the BH army, and where there was open ground such as just here where my marker is, that would be common area which would be no-man's land. But the summary is the Pale road belongs to the Serbs. Lower down belongs to the BH army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, if the witness could point out or even mark or somebody puts on the record where he is pointing to as he goes along.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I was about to ask that. If the witness could clarify what elevation is the one you referred to as occupied by the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said this is going uphill. The area that I've just ringed using a black marker pen is the road that I said is the Pale Road. I definitely know that this was under the control of the Serbian army. The letter H is high ground, that's high ground. That is high ground. The rest of it -- I've drawn a front line down here, but the actual specific front line I cannot be more accurate because it is in closely wooded area, and it was also extremely steep as there was a cliff near PAPA 6, so give an example. But the Serbian army was known to hold the high ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, to interrupt again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Perhaps the witness could draw a line, sort of a dotted line where you think the front line or where you are not sure where the front line is, to the fluid, or where it's located.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've drawn a dotted line in black ink, and it's between the area that's previously described as the Pale Road and the front line that I drew earlier on today. It was in this area that would become no-man's land. The trenches I observed were in thickly wooded area, but there is open ground as well. We did not go up the slope to try and find out exactly where the front line was; we just did it from our experience and from other observations.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Harding, can you mark on this map the locations from which, according to you, shots were fired by soldiers of the army of Republika Srpska at the town and at what parts of town? You talked about this yesterday. Could you mark it on the map, please, if you can. If not, tell us that you don't know.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whilst I was at PAPA 6, I observed a Serbian army battery. They were off this map to the east and on a hill. And I observed them as they shelled the PTT building. We timed the flight of their ammunition and the number of rounds that were fired, and they coincided exactly with what the PTT building was reporting to me. They fired about three volleys of at least two rounds. The reason I can specifically remember this is because we recorded the time of flight, which is standard operating procedure for the British forces, so that you know the round you see land on the ground is the round fired by the artillery that you are dealing with. And so I cannot mark this. They were on a ridge line off to the northeast from my position.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when this was?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to look through my diary if you need an exact date. But it would have been when PAPA 6 was in position and operational, so you're looking at November. Shall I look through my diary to give you an exact date?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you draw up a report about this incident?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: We recorded -- it became difficult to report on that because it should have been a ShootRep from the LIMA side if there had been a LIMA position there which I didn't know. So we would have recorded it as an incident report because the PTT had been shelled. I didn't need to forward this report to the PTT because I gave them the grid reference of the battery engaging them, and they could count the incoming rounds for themselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And based on the information you gave them, can you locate the direction in relation to this map of a hill where you say the battery was, in relation to the PTT building?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the PTT building, it was directly east.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you indicate this on the map so that we can orient ourselves, show us the part of town this refers to.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. The PTT building was on the main road leading into Sarajevo. It was receiving fire from there an approximate bearing of 160 degrees slightly less than east on the hill, which is off this map, if that answers your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Are you saying that this is behind the hill that you marked, that this was the high ground where the army of Republika Srpska was?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: The area I'm pointing to now is in the valley. High ground to the north, high ground for the south. There was a clear channel all the way down to the city and still in direct line of sight all the way down the road. This is in the valley. The ground then climbs because the valley turns from heading at 160 degrees grid it turns and heads away down to let's say 120 degrees grid and up. If you just move the map a little bit more, from the old city, you're going uphill. And this is high ground, and the battery I was observing from PAPA 6 across on to the high ground was in approximately this location. You see the ground is climbing there. That is the top of a hill, and it was in this area. And it could be seen on the crest of the hill. The reason I could identify it during the shelling of the PTT is the muzzle flashes were clearly visible on the ridge line. And so I could time 21 seconds from leaving the barrel to the impact. And that time was repeated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, if the witness again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think -- Ms. Pilipovic, would you please guide the witness to mark or describe exactly which spot he indicated.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the witness to go back to the end of this map and to read the part that can be seen so that we can orient ourselves as to the direction from which you say the shell came. If the witness could draw a dotted line from the location of the PTT building to the place where, in your estimation, the shots were fired from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, if the witness just indicates the place where he saw the fire came from, would that be enough? I mean a straight line could be mentioned by everyone and the map will be overloaded with all kind of markings.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
