utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you please assist us and put that part of the map on the screen by manipulating it on the ELMO so we can see how Mr. Harding will mark the source of the fire he saw.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I marked on the map two arrows pointing towards the west. The area concerned is slightly off this map. The arrows are drawn on the hill -- on the slope which is still climbing as it goes to the east. The arrows are also in woods where the artillery in question was not on the wood line; it was on the crest line. You could see the muzzle shots. It then fired down towards the PTT and the PTT was being shelled from the east.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what artillery piece was used?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: The specific type and calibre, you'd have to refer to somebody from the LIMA side as, although I have no evidence, I think they were Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. tasked to go and have a look to find out what had happened from the Bosnian Serb side of the incident. It would presume by the range, the accuracy, and the muzzle flash, it was probably a 122 millimetre artillery.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us the range of the 122 millimetre weapon?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you the range of that as I was only on the city. I had no reason to talk to anybody and I never saw any of that inside the city. I know it is a primary piece of artillery, and I in my previous experience have only dealt with the British 105 millimetre light gun, and they were static 155 weapons. So I can't tell you the range of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what damage was caused to the PTT building after the building was fired on from those positions. Can you tell us that?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't tell you that. You'd have to refer to one of the PTT staff. However, when I reported to the PTT building, it was fully functional and there was no significant damage to the structure.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether on the occasion of this incident a report was drawn up in the PTT?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, the PTT was my higher command. And what reports they generated I suspect would be a complaint to the Serbian liaison officer or down through LIMA side into Lukavica barracks. But that was a higher command for me, so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, yesterday during the examination-in-chief you mentioned an incident that happened on the 23rd of October at the cemetery. Can you tell us whether on that occasion in the area of the Lav Cemetery, PAPA 3 was in the immediate vicinity, and I am referring to the 23rd of October?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 23rd of October, my second in command was visiting the position in the former olympic stadium. We did not have a proper position adjacent to the Lion Cemetery at that time. As part of his patrol, he would stop there and check that the armoured vehicles had not moved and were still there. But no, we had nobody there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you are telling us that your deputy, along with you, was accommodated in the PAPA 3 premises which were near the olympic stadium?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't accommodated there. I was in the PAPA headquarters. And neither was my 2IC.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Apart from your 2IC, how many people were there at the PAPA 3 point?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: We always aimed to roster two people down there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: On the 23rd of October, with respect to the incident that was reported to you, did you get an official report as to the time and place of that incident and the positions from which shots were fired at the cemetery?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: My second in command would have filled out an incident report, and it would have been reported to the PTT in the normal way.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether on the 23rd of October, your second in command did fill in the form and sent the report?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did, because he then described what he had seen, and that generated me to go and visit that location the following day. I made note of it in my diary at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when and at what time on the 23rd of October you received the report from your second in command as to the incident that took place?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not record the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Are you saying that you received the report of the incident on that day?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He would have reported it on the 23rd, the day that he saw it, and that's the day I made note of it in my diary. Regarding timings, it was in broad daylight, and I cannot narrow it down to morning or afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And did the report contain a description of the positions from which shells were fired at the Lav Cemetery?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the north of the cemetery is the front line. The building was struck on its north-facing side, which is where the door was in the photographs that you saw. It was only a matter of a two-minute drive to the north before you're at the front line. We did not see from where the artillery or mortars that it was fired from. It was unexpected. So no, he would not have reported from where it came because he did not see where it came.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you are telling us that it was not in the report and that you do not know from what direction and from what positions the shelling of the cemetery, the Lav Cemetery, on the 23rd of October was carried out?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: The weapons came from the north. And any more than that would have been conjecture and just his opinion and we were only to report the facts of what we saw. So he would have just said "from the north."

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us on the basis of what you determined that the shelling came from the north? What in the military sense led you to conclude that the shots were fired from the north? And could you mark the direction on the map, please, north in relation to the cemetery.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I marked on the map in black pen an arrow with an N which is pointing towards the north. The Lion Cemetery and the stadium are to the west of the arrow that I've drawn. The reason we would say that the rounds came from the north is because that side of the building faces north, and the round landed at the base of the north-facing slope. Therefore, it would have been impossible to drop that round from any other direction, because there was hills to the east and it was open ground to the west. But the round would have had a strike mark pointing either east or west if it came from that location.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us in relation to the direction you have indicated whose army was concentrated there? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the map, going down the road towards the stadium, there were a lot of open ground, and the front line was in the approximate location of the blue dotted line that was drawn yesterday. It was open ground to the north of the blue dotted line were the Serbian army forces. To the south of the blue dotted line were the BH forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday, during the examination-in-chief you told us that in part of the PAPA 3 location near the Lion Cemetery, you saw armoured vehicles, and that you observed them. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us in relation to the cemetery, how far were these armoured vehicles away from the cemetery?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the east of PAPA 3 is an independent building, and these armoured vehicles were to the east and to the south. From my recollection, it was only about 200 metres on the south side of the building and slightly on the eastern side of the building. But it was on lower ground and you had to go through the building to see them.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether there were any soldiers in the building protecting the APCs? When I say soldiers, I'm referring to the BH army troops.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't see any.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In your opinion, can you tell us whether the place where the APCs were and the surrounding area constituted a military target?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: By their nature, you could say that the armoured vehicles were a military target. Regarding the surrounding area, I would say no because there was nothing at all of a military nature.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: During your tour of duty, do you know whether these armoured vehicles were used in certain operations by the BH army?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: The vehicles were checked twice a day, and up until the time I departed, they never moved.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So I gather that your testimony was that the vehicles were not used during your tour of duty?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I didn't see them, and it was not reported to me that they were moved which is why we moved the UNMOs from that location because they were not being used to the best effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, you told us that PAPA 4 was located near the Kosevo stadium. When was PAPA 4 located near the stadium Kosevo, in what period of time?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I arrived to the day I left, we always had UNMOs under the stadium.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you spoke about mortars, 82, 120, and 60 millimetres calibre which were located in the area where the hospital was. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't specify calibre. The staff sergeant who saw it didn't specify a calibre. But he had reported through his command that the mortars were fired around the hospital, within the environs of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the mortar activity from the hospital compound was reported by your colleagues and your superior officer at the time, Mr. Cutler?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army staff sergeant would have reported it and it eventually came to the Colonel, which is how I found out about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Harding, yesterday you spoke about the incident which occurred on the 24th of September, 1992, and told us, that is, provided description of the tanks which you said were moving south. I think the street in question is the one connecting Nedzarici and the airport, at least that is what you indicated on the map. Could you tell us now from what direction these tanks were moving towards Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: They came from the east. They were heading west. They then turned the corner and started to head north. They were going up the primary road that goes past Dobrinja, past Nedzarici, and off to the north.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that fire was opened from these tanks. Can you tell us whether you yourself observed the incident the way you described, or is it the case that somebody else told you about the incident?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I observed this myself because it was such a significant movement of armour, the biggest that I'd seen to date. And that's why I watched from the OP at PAPA 5. I personally watched it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Following this event, did you compile a report?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would have filled out the incident report at PAPA 5, which would have then been sent to PAPA headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you spoke about the incident which occurred on the 8th of December, 1992, and told us that the shelling started at 10.00 and lasted until 1600. The shells would have landed east of the headquarters where you were, if I understood your testimony correctly.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date you're referring to is the 31st of October, and that is correct. They were landing to the east and to the west of PAPA headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us and mark on the map the positions from which the shells came?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot say where the shells came as I did not see any of them firing. I was merely in the middle of when they landed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Was it possible for you, on the basis of the position of the shells that were falling in the area, to establish the direction from which they had come?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you'd have to talk to someone from LIMA side.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can I therefore conclude that you cannot confirm at this point that the shells had come from the positions under the BH army control, or from the positions under the VRS control?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot say where they came from.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, as a member of the United Nations and a military observer, did you have an obligation to visit the site where incidents occurred, specifically, would you visit the site of a sniping incident? I'm not referring to you personally, but to your service.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we would not report sniping activity as an incident. However, we would make note of where it was so that if we were going there, we could take appropriate precautions.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you visited the scene of an incident in cases you had been informed of an incident and an injury or a casualty, what type of activity would you undertake? What kind of obligations did you have? Did you have to file a report? Did you have to establish the positions from where the fire was open and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: The incidents that were seen by the observation posts were reported by the forms that I've previously described. If there was a specific incident, I would have been tasked by Colonel Mole or Colonel Cutler to go and attend the report in all respects. We were not there to decide who had instigated it or where the shots had come from if we couldn't see where they had come from. So there was very few incidents I was tasked to, but I would try to look at everything so that the Colonel had the facts and they were not biased to either side.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: During your tour of duty in Sarajevo as an UNMO, approximately how often would you visit the scenes of sniping incidents, and is it possible for you to describe for us one such incident and the measures that you undertook on those occasions?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sniping is regarded as small-arms fire and occurred all around the city all the time. So we did not report sniping activity as it could not be differentiated from the small-arms fire. If I did go to a sniping incident and there was only one, was where a woman was shot dead and was lying on the road to the west of PTT. We did not stop because of the risk from sniping. It was a French battalion armoured personal carrier that stopped and picked up the dead body, and I merely followed up that incident by identifying the casualty, seeing where she had been shot. I filled out a one-page report so that if the UNPROFOR were accused of helping the casualties of one side the answer was already in the PTT and it was merely on a more humanitarian reason, rather than taking a side.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Is it your testimony that in respect of that sniping incident, your team did not carry out an onsite investigation, nor did they investigate the firing position, that is, the position from which the shots were opened that hurt this woman? You merely assisted her?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, there was no specific onsite because it was considered too dangerous to stand there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: During your tour of duty in Sarajevo, you told us that there was sniping activity in the town. Were there any protests lodged by the warring factions with respect to the sniping activity, either you personally or someone from your team?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Since you were positioned in town and had a number of colleagues who patrolled around the town, were you at any point in time informed by them about any specific locations inside the town from which sniper fire was opened? Did you have any such information?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did. To the east of PAPA headquarters, there were signs on the corners of the road so that when you crossed that road, you knew that you had to move quickly as a sniper had been firing down that road. To the west, enroute to the PTT, we used the main carriageway, and it was not uncommon to be fired at when you crossed the road at junctions. And the fire would come from the south.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether you, as a United Nations military observer, had the obligation following an incident such as a shelling incident to verify the situation on the other side, depending on which side opened fire? Did you have any duty to establish the direction from which the fire came? That is, did you have to identify the side that opened fire? Was that one of your obligations, or is it the case that you only had to report on what you actually saw?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would report the incident when we saw shells landing. We would not say where they came from because you would be unable to tell when observing from a distance. The LIMA side would report firing from their positions. The collation of that information would have been one of the duties in the PTT headquarters, UNPROFOR headquarters. Whether they tried to establish the time of our reports of impacts to the time of their reports of ShootReps, I am unaware. But I know that they were severely undermanned to monitor the weapons around the outside of the city. If we were to say where the rounds came from, it would be personal opinion and conjecture which we didn't do.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You've just told us that you made record of the number of impacts. On the basis of what did you make your estimates of the number of impacts in the area that was shelled? What was the manner in which you proceeded?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Firstly, attention would be drawn to the area by the sound of the explosion. Then by looking at the area, either with the naked eye or binoculars, you would see the debris brought up by the explosion. It was presumed that the number of explosions would be the same as the number of rounds that landed on that position. So it was by hearing and observing that the reports were made.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: These reports that you made, were they accurate in terms of probability, or were they reports made on the basis of personal observation?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reports were made as observed by the military observer, and the accuracy would be he was required to give a 6-figure grid reference using the map that he was provided with.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday during the examination-in-chief by my learned colleague, you spoke about a multibarrel rocket launcher. On the map of the town, can you indicate for us the positions from which the soldiers of the VRS targeted the town and tell us which areas of the town were engaged by this multiple-barrel rocket launchers? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you would look at the map, I'm pointing to the position that was designated as PAPA 1, drawn on the map in blue ink with the number 1. On the incident that I think you're referring to, we had moved slightly around that hill. We were on the face that was facing towards the west, and we had observed some shelling, came back around the corner of that hill when the projectiles flew over our head. They were heading towards the city in the direction that the pointer is laid as a straight line. We just looked towards the city to see where they impacted, and we saw munitions landing to the east of the PAPA headquarters, which is just here. From that distance, we could only estimate how far to the east that you could see the rounds as they exploded on the rooftops to the east. To draw a backbearing to that, from the position we observed to the position of impact, they must have come from the northwest of the city. That would be, if I follow the pointer down, over towards the area of Zuc and north of that, somewhere in this area. That was how we presumed where they came from because we were in an unusual position to have been overflown by the projectiles and see where they landed. Therefore, we had two points which to draw a straight line between. Normally, when the ammunition lands, it's only a single point. You see the explosion so you don't know where it has come from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would it assist you, Ms. Pilipovic, if I indicated that the direction of the pointer the witness used was connecting the two lower left corners of the triangles marked yesterday as PAPA 1 and PAPA 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell us -- actually, did you tell us that it was from the direction of Zuc that a projectile was fired from a multiple rocket launcher? Is that what you indicated on the map?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: The launcher must have been located northwest of PAPA 2 because of the straight line. That line goes through where I've written on the map the area of Zuc which we spoke about earlier. This is a hilly area, and so it was somewhere maybe slightly to the north of where I wrote Z-U-C.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Whose troops were concentrated in the area of Zuc?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, that would be the -- possibly be the Serbian army. That precise date that I saw them, I would have to revise where the front line is drawn at the moment as BH forces had pushed their way through Zuc and moved the front sign. So I would need to reconsider exactly where the front line is, and also I have no experience of multi-barreled rocket launchers, so I do not know their range and any sighting requirements for them.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Just one more question: When was that? In what period of time while you were in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That happened on the 8th of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Was there already fighting going on in the area of Zuc?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the rounds flew over our heads, myself and Captain MacDonald had been observing shell fire on the hill directly west of our position. I'm indicating where we stood, just slightly west of the position marked as PAPA 1. Where the marker is, this is the bottom of the valley. This is the top of the valley, and there's a road just there. And they were shelling that road. Would you like me to somehow mark the map to show that?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, please. Would you please also tell us what was the period of time when this fighting for Zuc took place.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've marked a cross where we stood. I'm not quite sure how to mark it to delineate it from all the other markings on this map. I don't know what you would suggest. This is where we stood at the cross, and the road is marked by this black S-shaped line.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this, I think, would be a convenient time for a break. And I will also finish my cross-examination as far as this part is concerned, and my colleague will continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that would mean that we continue cross-examination tomorrow and we will now proceed to the examination-in-chief of the next witness? Would the Prosecution then prepare for examining the next witness. We'll then adjourn until 10 minutes to 1.00. Mr. Harding, you may have noticed, for all kind of practical reasons, your cross-examination and a possible re-examination by the Prosecution will take place tomorrow. I know it's very inconvenient for you, but we are more or less forced to do it this way as you might have misunderstood. We apologise for that. So your presence is not needed any more today, but tomorrow morning at 9.00 we'll start again in this same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was due to return to the United Kingdom at 1600 hours today. I would need to sort out flights. Also, I have a four-year-old son back in the United Kingdom being looked after by a platoon of relatives. So I need to have a little look at that and see if I'm able to do that or if I have to stay here, my wife and myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I was, as a matter of fact, expecting that this would have been discussed with you by the Prosecution. But it now turns that it has not been because this is more or less the schedule we arranged for yesterday. Perhaps it would have been wiser to keep you in the courtroom instead of discussing the matter in your absence. Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I had caused some inquiries to be made of the Victims and Witnesses Unit as to whether it would impact on the witness and I apologise. I had not received word back. That may be a team issue, rather than a victims witness issue. In order to accommodate the witness, Mr. President, I would have no -- the Prosecution would have no problem with the witness returning to the UK, and then coming back to The Hague at a later date for further cross-examination. In fact, given that Mr. Kucanin has been waiting around for over an week, that would enable us to continue with his evidence uninterrupted and provide more time to Mr. Piletta-Zanin to finally hone into his cross-examination so he fits within the remaining half an hour or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see that Ms. Pilipovic is nodding that she would agree. Let's then -- if you'd just discuss when the witness could be recalled to further be cross-examined and inform this Chamber as soon as possible. You'll understand that the Chamber has yet put any questions to the witness, and I think that the less time we'll have in between the continuation of the cross-examination and the breakup today of the cross-examination, the better it would be. And Ms. Pilipovic, you'd like to add something?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to say that the Defence understands the problems that Mr. Harding is faced with, with his family. So whenever you decide to recall Mr. Harding for further cross-examination, we agree with that. We will be ready to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So could you please arrange, then, Mr. Ierace, that it would be as soon as possible, perhaps after we finish the examination and cross-examination of Mr. Kucanin. Yes. Then we'll adjourn until 5 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do apologise that the Chamber took some ten minutes extra which was necessary to discuss a matter of the order which have no consequences for the order at this moment, but that's the reason why we are back a bit later than indicated. Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I spoke to Mr. Harding, of course strictly in relation to him returning to the Tribunal, during the break. And he has told me that he will attempt to return to The Hague so that he's in a position to continue his evidence on Thursday. I anticipate that that will follow the evidence of Mr. Kucanin. He has an estimate of three hours in chief. It's also been brought to my attention during the break that [redacted] who was to be called immediately following Mr. Kucanin is now seeking some protective measures. I would be grateful if we could make an oral application, perhaps a little before we adjourn. That will be done by Chester Stamp of the Prosecution team. Essentially, the request relates to some issues which perhaps should be pursued in closed session. Indeed, on reflection, I would respectfully ask that his name be redacted. The application can be expanded on at a later point, if that's convenient to the Trial Chamber. Mr. President, all of that being said, I'm now in a position to commence the examination-in-chief of Mirsad Kucanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, would this mean that you would like to have redacted the name of the witness you just mentioned on the record of today?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, please. In case the application is successful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I remind you, talking about protective measures, that I think at the beginning of March we expect some witnesses to be heard where I think no final decisions have yet been taken on the protective measures and we are still waiting for some information. Would you please check that, because that's my recollection. I'm not specifically prepared to make this remark at this very moment, but since you talked about protective measures it comes into my mind. Yes, then, yes, I was interrupting you, Mr. Ierace, I see in the transcript. "In case the application was successful," yes, that was your last remark. We are at the moment where we can call your next witness. Mr. Usher, would you please bring the witness into the courtroom. Perhaps I may remind the parties if we want to continue the cross-examination of Mr. Harding on Thursday, we have approximately half an hour to go today. If you'd stay within the time limits, you'd use two and a half hours tomorrow, which would leave us two more hours tomorrow for the cross-examination, and we would then still have one hour for the cross-examination on Thursday. But as soon as we have whatever kind of delays we might not be able to finish the cross-examination of Mr. Harding by Thursday. So may I specifically urge the parties to behave as disciplined as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I've just received an email from a member of my team who tells me that Mr. Kucanin will not be available to the Trial Chamber for another 15 minutes. I don't know what the reason is for that. But that being the case, perhaps we could make some use of this time by me raising an issue that will arise in any event during the examination-in-chief of Mr. Kucanin. Mr. President, this witness has made three statements to the investigators of the office of the Prosecution. Those statements, of course, have been disclosed to the Defence. In one of those statements, being a statement made on the 12th of November, 1995, the witness at great length referred to a number of positions around Sarajevo. The witness was a criminal inspector, that is, a member of the police force, during the armed conflict in Sarajevo. And consequently investigated a large number of incidents where civilians were the victims of small-arms fire or shelling. As a result of his general experience, in that statement, he listed a large number of places where in his opinion sniping originated on the Bosnian Serb army side of the confrontation line. And similarly, where shelling originated on the Bosnian Serb army of the confrontation line. Had he been required to mark those positions during his evidence, I anticipate he would have taken in excess of an hour just to do that. Therefore, out of Court, he has marked a map with those various positions. The Defence was notified of our intention to seek to tender that map by letter dated I think the 21st of February, and copies of the map were served at that time. Yes, the 21st of February. Mr. President, if we're allowed to follow that course, then we should comfortably conclude his evidence within the three hours. I should think well within the three hours, so perhaps whilst we await Mr. Kucanin's arrival, the Defence could perhaps indicate if they have any difficulty with that. Secondly, I note that Mr. Stamp is now present, and he could elaborate in closed session on the situation in relation to the aforementioned witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, would you please first respond to the request of Mr. Ierace to extender into evidence a premarked map with all the positions.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, at present the Defence has only the statement of the 10th and 12th of November, 1995. As for the rest of the file, it is with my colleague, because he is expected Mr. Mirsad Kucanin to testify on Thursday. So I don't have the map in front of me, and I cannot give you my answer now. I will be able to do so tomorrow morning before we begin. All I have is a statement of the 10th of November, 1995, and a few official notes, but I do not have the map in front of me so I cannot discuss it now. With your permission, the Defence would like to respond tomorrow morning before the examination resumes, because my colleague was preparing to examine Mr. Kucanin on Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not expressing the opinion of the Chamber on what our decision would be even if we would allow you to respond tomorrow morning. I think we should keep in mind that being surprised during the examination-in-chief by a map slowly being marked over one hour might not be a situation where the Defence is better off. But let's just hear tomorrow from Mr. Piletta-Zanin briefly what his opinion is about the production of this map, this premarked map. I must say that I do appreciate that for time-saving reasons some pretrial marking is done because this morning, I noticed that even the direction north on a map still had to be marked, which seemed perhaps a bit superfluous. I understand that the witness is not yet available, so then Mr. Stamp could explain to us the reasons for the protective measures. So we have to go into closed session. Private would be enough, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 1.29 p.m., to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 27th day of February, 2000, at 9.00 a.m.
